content:
"Amazing love! How can it be that thou, my God, shouldst die for me?" Charles Wesley's hymn of 1738 puts into song a belief that runs deep in Christian devotion: that on the cross, God died. Muslims answer that the scriptures of both faiths say the opposite.

God is the Living, the Everlasting, the one who cannot die. A death of God would be a contradiction in terms.

The question came up again in a recent public debate between a Muslim speaker and a panel of Christians, and it deserves a careful answer. The seven answers below set out what the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament and the Quran say about God's life, how the church answered the question, and what follows from each answer.

The belief is old. Melito of Sardis, a bishop of the second century, wrote of the crucifixion: "He who hung the earth is hanging; he who fixed the heavens has been fixed... God has been murdered." Acts 20:28 speaks of "the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood."[1]

Most Christian theologians would add a qualification at once. They do not say that the divine nature ceased to exist for three days. They say that the eternal Son took a human nature, and that in that nature he truly died; because the one who died is God the Son, it can be said that "God died." This is the form of the claim to be weighed, and the answers below weigh it.[1]

The Hebrew Bible describes a God whose life has no beginning and no end. "Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God" (Psalm 90:2).

God swears by His own unending life: "As I live forever" (Deuteronomy 32:40). "For I the LORD do not change" (Malachi 3:6).[2]

Muslim speakers often cite Habakkuk 1:12, and honesty requires a note on it. The English Standard Version reads: "Are you not from everlasting, O LORD my God, my Holy One? We shall not die." The rabbis listed this verse among the "corrections of the scribes" (tiqqune soferim), places where scribes are said to have softened a phrase out of reverence, and they record that the original read "You shall not die." On either reading, the verse addresses God as the one "from everlasting." The point it makes about God does not depend on the variant.[2]

Isaiah adds the language of strength: "The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary" (Isaiah 40:28). The psalmist sets the creation's end against God's endlessness: "They will perish, but you will remain... you are the same, and your years have no end" (Psalm 102:26-27). A God who does not grow weary does not die.[2]

The New Testament repeats the teaching in the plainest words. Paul blesses "the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God" (1 Timothy 1:17).

He writes of God as the one "who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light" (1 Timothy 6:16). The word translated "immortal" means "not subject to death."[3]

The Hebrew Bible had already drawn the line between God and man: "God is not man, that he should lie" (Numbers 23:19); "for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst" (Hosea 11:9). A being who dies is, by that fact, on the human side of the line.[3]

A related argument concerns place. At the dedication of the temple, Solomon prays: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!" (1 Kings 8:27; 2 Chronicles 6:18).

Isaiah gives God's own words: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me?" (Isaiah 66:1). Paul quotes the same thought in Athens: God "does not live in temples made by man" (Acts 17:24).[4]

Christians reply that God can be present in a special way without being contained, as He was in the temple. The reply is fair as far as it goes. But a body that walks, sleeps and dies is contained in a place in the plainest sense, and Solomon's question was asked of a building far grander than a human frame.

The church faced the question directly. Cyril of Alexandria, in the twelfth of his anathemas against Nestorius in 430, condemned anyone who would not confess that "the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh." The Second Council of Constantinople in 553 condemned anyone who denied that the crucified Lord is "one of the holy Trinity."[5]

The answer rests on the doctrine of two natures, and it carries a cost either way it is read. If the divine nature did not die, and only the human nature died, then God, as God, did not die, and the death on the cross was the death of a man. If the divine nature did die, then the scriptures quoted above are contradicted.

The formula "God died in the flesh" holds the two together in words. A reader may fairly ask whether it does more than restate the difficulty.

The church itself drew a line here. In the early third century some teachers in Rome said that the Father had suffered on the cross. Tertullian wrote Against Praxeas to refute them, and the view, later called patripassianism, was rejected as heresy.

The church therefore agreed that God the Father cannot suffer or die. It kept the claim only for the Son, and only "in the flesh." Each refinement moves the death further from God and closer to the man.[5]

Even the verse most often cited is uncertain. In Acts 20:28 several important manuscripts read "the church of the Lord" in place of "the church of God," and the English Standard Version notes that the closing words can be read "with the blood of his Own," meaning his own Son.[1]

The death of God is usually tied to a second claim: that it pays for the sins of others. The speaker in the debate offered an image: a judge facing a guilty man, who says, "Here is my innocent son; I will punish him, and you may go free." No court on earth would call that justice.

The Hebrew Bible agrees with the court. "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin" (Deuteronomy 24:16).

"The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father" (Ezekiel 18:20). "He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD" (Proverbs 17:15).[6]

The Quran states the same law: "No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (6:164; 53:38). In al-Faruqi's reading, man begins "ethically sane and sound, not weighed down by any original sin," and needs no one to pay his debt; he answers for his own deeds and hopes in God's mercy. The site's article on ransom in the Bible and the Quran takes the question further.[6][7]

The Quran gives God a name that answers the question in advance: "Rely on the Living who does not die" (25:58). The Throne Verse opens: "God, there is no god but He, the Living, the Sustainer of all. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep" (2:255). Everything else ends: "Everyone upon it will perish, and there remains the Face of your Lord, full of majesty and honour" (55:26-27).[8]

The Quran draws the consequence for Jesus with a gentle precision: "The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. His mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food" (5:75). A being who needs food, and who can die, is a creature. On the crucifixion itself the Quran says that "they did not kill him and they did not crucify him" (4:157), and the site's article on what the Quran says about the crucifixion sets out that verse and its readings.

The companions met the same question on the day the Prophet died. Umar, overcome, refused to believe it. Abu Bakr came, kissed the Prophet's face, and went out to the people: "Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead; and whoever worshipped God, God is living and does not die." Then he recited: "You will die, and they will die" (39:30), and "Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him" (3:144).

The honour of a messenger, however great, does not lift him out of death; God alone is the Living.[8] Al-Faruqi's first principle is the line the whole question turns on: God and creature are two orders, and "it is forever impossible that the one be united with, infused, confused with or diffused into the other."[7][8]

The bottom line

The Hebrew Bible calls God everlasting and unchanging; the New Testament calls Him immortal, the only one who has immortality; Solomon says that heaven itself cannot contain Him. The church answered that God died "in the flesh," and that formula either leaves the divine nature untouched, so that the one who died was a man, or makes God mortal, against the scriptures. The idea that an innocent can die so that the guilty go free runs against the law of Moses and the words of Ezekiel.

The Quran's answer is short. God is the Living who does not die, and Jesus, honoured as His messenger, was a man who ate food. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Charles Wesley, "And Can It Be" (1738). Melito of Sardis, On Pascha 96. Acts 20:28, with the ESV notes on the variant "of the Lord" and the reading "with the blood of his Own". Bible quotations follow the English Standard Version.
  2. Psalm 90:2; Deuteronomy 32:40; Malachi 3:6; Isaiah 40:28; Psalm 102:26–27; Habakkuk 1:12. On the tiqqune soferim, including Habakkuk 1:12, see Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd edition (Minneapolis: Fortress, 2012), on the corrections of the scribes.
  3. 1 Timothy 1:17; 6:16; Numbers 23:19; Hosea 11:9.
  4. 1 Kings 8:27; 2 Chronicles 6:18; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 17:24.
  5. Tertullian, Against Praxeas 1–2 and 29; Cyril of Alexandria, Third Letter to Nestorius, anathema 12; the Second Council of Constantinople (553), anathema 10; in Norman P. Tanner (ed.), Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, vol. 1 (London: Sheed and Ward; Washington: Georgetown University Press, 1990).
  6. Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20; Proverbs 17:15; Quran 6:164; 53:38.
  7. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1.
  8. Quran 25:58; 2:255; 55:26–27; 5:75; 4:157; 39:30; 3:144. Sahih al-Bukhari 3668, report of A'isha.
